dx: Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction from left anterior descending artery occlusion
case: A 61-year-old man with hypertension and a 40 pack-year smoking history comes to the emergency department 4 hours after crushing substernal chest pain began. The pain radiates to his left arm, and he is diaphoretic. Pulse is 102/min, and blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg. The ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads V1 to V4. Serum troponin I is 8.2 ng/mL (reference below 0.04 ng/mL). Echocardiography shows no motion of the anterior wall, anterior septum, and apex of the left ventricle, with an ejection fraction of 40% (normal 55 to 70%). Diagnosis: acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).

questions.stem: Occlusion of which of the following arteries most likely explains the ST-segment elevation in leads V1 to V4 and the loss of anterior wall, septal, and apical motion?
options: Left anterior descending artery
Right coronary artery
Left circumflex artery
Posterior interventricular artery
approach: Match the leads to the wall: V1 and V2 face the septum, and V3 and V4 face the anterior wall.
Recall which artery runs down the anterior interventricular groove to the apex.
That artery, the LAD, supplies the anterior left ventricle, the apex, and the anterior two-thirds of the septum.
questions.why: The left anterior descending artery is a branch of the left main coronary artery that runs in the anterior interventricular groove toward the apex. It supplies the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the apex, and the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum through its septal branches. ST elevation in V1 to V4 with anterior and apical wall motion loss is the classic pattern of LAD occlusion, the most common site of coronary occlusion in MI.
whyNot: Correct.
The right coronary artery supplies the right ventricle and, in most people, the inferior wall, the SA node, and the AV node. Its occlusion causes ST elevation in the inferior leads II, III, and aVF.
The left circumflex artery runs in the left atrioventricular groove and supplies the lateral and posterior left ventricle. Its occlusion shows up in the lateral leads I, aVL, V5, and V6.

The posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery usually arises from the right coronary artery and supplies the inferior wall and the posterior third of the septum, which leads V1 to V4 do not face.

topics: ECG leads and the walls they face

questions.stem: Troponin I is a structural protein of the myocyte contractile apparatus. Which of the following processes is most likely responsible for its increased serum concentration in this patient?
options: Exocytosis of troponin by viable myocytes under stress
Membrane rupture in myocytes that have died by necrosis
Caspase-driven apoptosis of myocytes in the ischemic zone
Hepatic synthesis of troponin as an acute phase reactant
approach: Note that troponin normally sits inside the myocyte, bound to the thin filaments.
Ask what lets an intracellular protein reach the blood: loss of plasma membrane integrity.
Membrane breakdown is the hallmark of irreversible injury and necrosis.
questions.why: After about 20 to 40 minutes of severe ischemia, myocyte injury becomes irreversible. ATP loss, calcium influx, and activation of phospholipases and proteases damage the plasma membrane, so the cell contents leak out. Troponin I and troponin T are cardiac-specific, so their leakage into blood marks myocyte necrosis. Troponin begins to rise within about 2 to 4 hours and stays elevated for about 7 to 10 days.
whyNot: Myocytes do not package troponin into vesicles for secretion. A large rise like his reflects leakage from dead cells.
Correct.
Apoptosis keeps the plasma membrane intact, and the cell fragments are eaten by macrophages without spilling their contents. The cell death of an infarct is mainly coagulative necrosis.
The liver does not make cardiac troponin. Acute phase reactants made by the liver include C-reactive protein and fibrinogen.

questions.stem: Two days after the onset of pain, he dies of ventricular fibrillation. Which of the following microscopic findings is most likely in the infarcted anterior wall at autopsy?
options: Macrophages clearing dead myocytes at the infarct border
Granulation tissue with new capillaries and fibroblasts
Coagulative necrosis with a dense neutrophil infiltrate
Dense collagen scar replacing the lost muscle fibers
approach: Note the timing: about 48 hours after the infarct began.
Recall the Robbins sequence: neutrophils peak at about 1 to 3 days, macrophages at about 3 to 7 days, granulation tissue at about 7 to 14 days, then scar.
At 2 days, expect dead myocytes with preserved outlines and many neutrophils.
questions.why: Myocardial infarcts undergo coagulative necrosis: dead myocytes keep their outlines while their nuclei fade. Neutrophils are drawn into the dead tissue and peak at about 1 to 3 days. Macrophages take over at about 3 to 7 days, granulation tissue forms at about 7 to 14 days, and a collagen scar matures over the following weeks. At 2 days the expected picture is coagulative necrosis with a dense neutrophil infiltrate.
whyNot: Macrophages arrive and begin removing dead myocytes at about 3 to 7 days. At 2 days the infiltrate is still mainly neutrophils.
Granulation tissue forms at the infarct margins at about 7 to 14 days.
Correct.
A collagen scar replaces the infarct over several weeks and is largely complete by about 2 months.

questions.stem: During the first hours, potassium released from injured cells depolarizes the resting membrane potential of myocytes at the infarct border from about -90 mV to about -65 mV. Which of the following best explains the slowed impulse conduction through these ventricular myocytes?
options: L-type calcium channels close early, so the phase 2 plateau is lost
Delayed rectifier potassium channels fail, so phase 3 is prolonged
Funny current channels open, so phase 4 depolarization speeds up
Many fast sodium channels stay inactivated, so phase 0 is slower
approach: Identify the ventricular myocyte upstroke (phase 0): rapid sodium influx through voltage-gated fast sodium channels.
Recall that these channels inactivate with sustained depolarization and recover only at a negative resting potential.
A less negative resting potential leaves fewer channels available, so the upstroke is smaller and slower, and conduction slows.
questions.why: The rapid upstroke of the ventricular myocyte action potential comes from sodium rushing in through voltage-gated fast sodium channels. These channels close an inactivation gate when the membrane stays depolarized and need a negative resting potential to reset. When extracellular potassium rises in ischemic tissue, the resting potential becomes less negative, many sodium channels stay inactivated, and phase 0 becomes smaller and slower. Slow conduction in the border zone sets up reentry, which is why ventricular fibrillation is a common cause of early death after MI.
whyNot: Calcium entry through L-type channels holds up the plateau and triggers contraction. It does not set how fast the upstroke spreads in ventricular myocytes.
Potassium efflux in phase 3 repolarizes the cell and sets the refractory period. It has no role in the speed of the upstroke.
The funny current drives spontaneous phase 4 depolarization in SA node cells. Working ventricular myocytes have a stable phase 4 and rely on sodium channels for their upstroke.
Correct.

dx: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia with coronary atherosclerosis and stable angina
case: A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of chest pressure that occurs when he climbs stairs and resolves with rest within 5 minutes. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 44 years. Physical examination shows firm nodules on both Achilles tendons. Fasting serum studies show LDL cholesterol 310 mg/dL (desirable below 100 mg/dL), HDL cholesterol 44 mg/dL (40 or higher), and triglycerides 120 mg/dL (below 150 mg/dL). An exercise stress test shows ischemic ST-segment depression. Coronary angiography shows 75% atherosclerotic narrowing of the proximal right coronary artery. Genetic testing shows one pathogenic variant in the LDL receptor gene and one normal copy. Diagnosis: heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia with coronary atherosclerosis and stable angina.

questions.stem: His LDL cholesterol is markedly increased, but his triglyceride concentration is normal. Which of the following is the direct consequence of his LDL receptor defect?
options: The liver makes and secretes more VLDL than usual
Lipoprotein lipase in capillaries is less active
Less LDL is taken up and cleared by hepatocytes
HDL can no longer carry cholesterol back to the liver
approach: Note the pattern: isolated high LDL with normal triglycerides.
Recall that most LDL leaves the blood by receptor-mediated endocytosis into hepatocytes through the LDL receptor.
A defective receptor means LDL stays in the blood longer and its level rises.
questions.why: Hepatocytes remove most LDL from the blood by binding its apolipoprotein B-100 to the LDL receptor and taking it in by receptor-mediated endocytosis. In familial hypercholesterolemia, an autosomal dominant defect in the LDL receptor slows this clearance, so plasma LDL rises, often 2 to 3 times normal in heterozygotes. The excess LDL deposits in tendons as xanthomas and in arteries as atheroma, which explains his early coronary disease.
whyNot: More VLDL output would raise fasting triglycerides as well as LDL. His triglycerides are normal, and an LDL receptor defect does not drive VLDL synthesis.
Low lipoprotein lipase activity causes high triglycerides from retained chylomicrons and VLDL (familial chylomicronemia). It does not raise LDL alone.
Correct.
Reverse cholesterol transport by HDL uses other receptors, such as scavenger receptor B1. His HDL is normal.

questions.stem: He begins statin therapy, and 8 weeks later his LDL cholesterol concentration has decreased by 45%. Which of the following best explains this decrease?
options: It blocks lipoprotein lipase, so less LDL is formed from VLDL in the blood
It blocks cholesterol esterase in the gut, so less dietary cholesterol is absorbed
It blocks 7-alpha-hydroxylase, so the liver converts more cholesterol to bile
It blocks HMG-CoA reductase, so his normal allele makes more LDL receptors
approach: Name the statin target: HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis (HMG-CoA to mevalonate).
Follow the effect in the hepatocyte: less cholesterol inside the cell activates SREBP, which turns on LDL receptor gene transcription.
Apply it to him: his one normal LDL receptor allele can still respond, so LDL clearance rises.
questions.why: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme that converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate in hepatic cholesterol synthesis. When hepatocyte cholesterol falls, the transcription factor SREBP increases expression of the LDL receptor gene, so the liver pulls more LDL out of the blood. In heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia the normal allele can be upregulated, so statins work well. Patients with two nonfunctional LDL receptor alleles respond poorly for this reason.
whyNot: Blocking lipoprotein lipase would raise triglycerides and is not how statins work. Statins inhibit the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis.
Reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption is how ezetimibe works, through the NPC1L1 transporter. Statins act on hepatic cholesterol synthesis.
7-alpha-hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of bile acid synthesis. Blocking it would leave more cholesterol in the liver, and statins do not target it.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the lipoprotein particle and the route by which dietary triglyceride leaves his small intestine after a fatty meal?
options: Chylomicrons, through lacteals and the thoracic duct
Chylomicrons, through the portal vein to the liver
VLDL particles, through lacteals and the thoracic duct
LDL particles, through the portal vein to the liver
approach: Identify the particle the enterocyte builds for dietary triglyceride: the chylomicron, with apolipoprotein B-48.
Recall that chylomicrons are too large for blood capillaries and enter the central lacteal of each villus.
Trace the lymph: lacteals, cisterna chyli, thoracic duct, and the left venous angle.
questions.why: Enterocytes package absorbed dietary triglyceride and cholesterol into chylomicrons containing apolipoprotein B-48. Chylomicrons are too large to pass into blood capillaries, so they enter the lacteals and reach the blood through the thoracic duct at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins. In the blood, lipoprotein lipase removes their triglyceride for muscle and fat, and the remnants are taken up by the liver.
whyNot: Correct.
Chylomicrons are too large to enter intestinal capillaries, so they do not travel in the portal vein. Short- and medium-chain fatty acids are the dietary fats that go by the portal route.
VLDL is made by the liver to export triglyceride the liver itself synthesizes. It does not carry dietary fat out of the intestine.
LDL is formed in the blood from VLDL after its triglyceride is removed. It does not carry dietary fat from the gut.

questions.stem: Macrophages in his coronary plaque are filled with cholesterol despite his defective LDL receptors. Which of the following best explains how cholesterol accumulated in his plaque?
options: Medial smooth muscle calcifies, and the stiff wall traps LDL from the plasma within it
Oxidized intimal LDL is taken up by macrophage scavenger receptors
Adventitial fibroblasts multiply, and LDL enters the wall from the vasa vasorum
Fibrin forms on normal endothelium, and LDL is trapped in the clot as it organizes
approach: Recall that atherosclerosis begins with endothelial injury or dysfunction in the intima.
LDL enters the intima and is oxidized; monocytes enter and become macrophages.
Macrophages take up oxidized LDL through scavenger receptors, which are separate from the LDL receptor, so foam cells form even in familial hypercholesterolemia.
questions.why: Atherosclerosis starts when injured or dysfunctional endothelium lets LDL into the intima, where it is oxidized. Recruited monocytes become macrophages that take up oxidized LDL through scavenger receptors, which do not depend on the LDL receptor and are not turned off by cholesterol in the cell. Engorged macrophages become foam cells, and smooth muscle cells migrate from the media into the intima and lay down collagen. The result is a fibrous cap over a lipid core. High LDL speeds up every step.
whyNot: Calcification of the media without lipid or inflammation is Monckeberg medial sclerosis. It does not narrow the lumen or form foam cells.
Correct.
Atherosclerosis is a disease of the intima. LDL enters from the lumen through injured endothelium, and the adventitia is not the site of plaque.
Thrombus usually forms on a plaque after its cap is disrupted. It does not start atherosclerosis on healthy endothelium.

dx: Rheumatic mitral stenosis with a past subacute endocarditis and current acute Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis
case: A 34-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 4-day history of fever. At age 9 years, she had fever, migratory polyarthritis, and a new heart murmur about 3 weeks after an untreated sore throat. She has known mitral stenosis with a valve area of 1.3 cm2 (normal 4 to 6 cm2). Three years ago, 2 weeks after a tooth extraction, she had 6 weeks of low-grade fever and fatigue, and a vegetation was found on her mitral valve; that infection was cured. She currently injects heroin. Her temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F). Physical examination shows a new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases in intensity with inspiration. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Diagnosis: rheumatic mitral stenosis, a past subacute endocarditis, and acute S. aureus endocarditis.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms most likely caused the pharyngitis that preceded her childhood illness?
options: Streptococcus agalactiae (group B)
Streptococcus pyogenes (group A)
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Staphylococcus aureus
approach: Recognize the childhood picture as acute rheumatic fever: carditis and migrating polyarthritis a few weeks after pharyngitis.
Recall that rheumatic fever follows throat infection with group A beta-hemolytic streptococci.
Name the organism: Streptococcus pyogenes.
questions.why: Acute rheumatic fever is a delayed, nonsuppurative complication of pharyngitis caused by group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes). It usually starts about 2 to 4 weeks after the sore throat, most often in children aged 5 to 15. Repeated or severe attacks scar the valves, and the mitral valve is affected most often. Prompt antibiotic treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis prevents rheumatic fever.
whyNot: Group B streptococci colonize the vagina and cause sepsis and meningitis in newborns. They do not cause pharyngitis followed by rheumatic fever.
Correct.
Pneumococcus causes pneumonia, otitis media, and meningitis. It is not linked to rheumatic fever.
S. aureus can cause many infections, but it does not trigger rheumatic fever. Her current endocarditis is a separate, later problem.

questions.stem: No bacteria were present in her heart during the childhood illness, yet her mitral valve was damaged and later scarred. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this valve damage?
options: Antibodies to streptococcal M protein bind valve proteins
IgE on mast cells triggers degranulation within the valve tissue
Circulating immune complexes deposit in the valve and fix complement
Streptococci invade the valve leaflets and form a small abscess
approach: Note that the valve is sterile, so the damage is immune mediated.
Recall molecular mimicry: streptococcal M protein resembles proteins in heart valves and myocardium.
Antibodies made against the bacterium bind the patient's own tissue, which is type II hypersensitivity.
questions.why: Rheumatic fever is an example of molecular mimicry. Antibodies made against the streptococcal M protein cross-react with similar proteins in the heart, including valve glycoproteins and myosin, which is classified as type II (antibody-mediated) hypersensitivity. CD4 T cells that react to the same antigens add to the inflammation. Aschoff bodies in the myocardium are the characteristic lesion, and repeated attacks leave the mitral valve thick, fused, and stenotic.
whyNot: Correct.
IgE and mast cell degranulation is type I hypersensitivity, as in anaphylaxis and allergic asthma. It does not scar heart valves.
Immune complex deposition is type III hypersensitivity. After streptococcal infection it explains poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, not rheumatic carditis.
Rheumatic fever is nonsuppurative: the valve is sterile. Bacteria growing on a valve would be infective endocarditis.

questions.stem: Her endocarditis 3 years ago began 2 weeks after a tooth extraction and followed an indolent 6-week course on her scarred mitral valve. Which of the following best explains that infection?
options: Staphylococcus aureus from the skin invaded the normal leaflets of the valve
Enterococcus faecalis from the bowel reached the valve after a colonoscopy
Candida albicans from a central line grew on the surface of the valve
Oral viridans streptococci adhered to fibrin on the scarred valve
approach: Note the clues: a slow, low-grade illness (subacute), a previously damaged valve, and recent dental work.
Recall that oral viridans streptococci enter the blood during dental procedures.
They adhere to the sterile fibrin and platelet deposits that form on damaged valve endothelium, using surface dextran and adhesins.
questions.why: Viridans streptococci, such as Streptococcus sanguinis and Streptococcus mutans, are normal mouth flora that enter the blood during dental work. They are low in virulence, so they usually infect valves that are already damaged, where small sterile fibrin and platelet deposits give them a place to attach. Dextran on their surface helps them stick. The illness develops over weeks to months, which is the classic subacute endocarditis pattern.
whyNot: S. aureus is highly virulent, can infect normal valves, and causes an acute illness over days. Her infection was slow and sat on a valve that was already damaged.
Enterococci cause subacute endocarditis after gastrointestinal or genitourinary procedures. Her infection followed dental work.
Fungal endocarditis is linked to central lines, prosthetic valves, and injection drug use. She had none of these at that time, and the trigger was a tooth extraction.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following valves is most likely the site of her current vegetation?
options: Mitral valve
Aortic valve
Tricuspid valve
Pulmonary valve
approach: Note that injected bacteria enter the venous blood and reach the right heart valves first.
A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration is right-sided regurgitation.
Inspiration raises venous return to the right heart, so right-sided murmurs get louder. The valve is the tricuspid.
questions.why: In people who inject drugs, bacteria and particles enter the veins and strike the tricuspid valve first, and S. aureus is the most common organism. Damage to the leaflets causes tricuspid regurgitation, a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, which increases venous return to the right heart and makes right-sided murmurs louder. Pieces of a tricuspid vegetation travel to the lungs as septic emboli.
whyNot: The mitral valve is the most common site of endocarditis in people who do not inject drugs. A mitral regurgitation murmur is loudest at the apex and does not increase with inspiration.
Aortic regurgitation gives a diastolic murmur along the left sternal border, and left-sided murmurs do not get louder with inspiration.
Correct.
Pulmonary valve endocarditis is rare. Its murmurs are heard at the left upper sternal border.

topics: Endocarditis in people who inject drugs

dx: Hypertensive heart disease with concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, and an aneurysm of the ascending aorta and arch
case: A 71-year-old man with 30 years of poorly controlled hypertension comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of hoarseness and difficulty swallowing solid food. Blood pressure is 172/98 mm Hg. Serum creatinine concentration is 1.7 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3 mg/dL) with mild proteinuria. Echocardiography shows a non-dilated left ventricle with a wall thickness of 15 mm (normal 6 to 11 mm), an ejection fraction of 62% (normal 55 to 70%), and impaired relaxation in diastole. CT shows a 6.2 cm aneurysm of the ascending aorta and aortic arch. Diagnosis: hypertensive heart disease with concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, and an aneurysm of the ascending aorta and arch.

questions.stem: Which of the following processes best explains his echocardiographic findings?
options: Eccentric hypertrophy from chronic volume overload
Dilated cardiomyopathy with failing contraction
Constrictive pericarditis that limits filling
Concentric hypertrophy from pressure overload
approach: Identify the load: long-standing hypertension raises afterload, which is a pressure overload.
Apply the Laplace relationship: wall stress rises with pressure and falls as the wall thickens.
Myocytes add sarcomeres in parallel, the wall thickens without dilation, and the stiff wall relaxes poorly.
questions.why: Chronic hypertension forces the left ventricle to generate high pressure. By the Laplace relationship, wall stress rises with pressure and radius and falls with wall thickness, so myocytes add sarcomeres in parallel and the wall thickens to bring stress back down. This is concentric hypertrophy. The thick, stiff wall fills poorly in diastole, so ejection fraction stays normal at first while relaxation is impaired. Over many years, the hypertrophied heart can dilate and fail.
whyNot: Volume overload, as in mitral or aortic regurgitation, adds sarcomeres in series. The chamber dilates and the wall is not much thicker than normal.
Dilated cardiomyopathy gives a large, thin-walled ventricle with a low ejection fraction. His ejection fraction is normal and the cavity is not dilated.
A stiff pericardium limits filling, but the myocardium itself is not thickened. His problem is in the ventricular wall.
Correct.

questions.stem: Compression of which of the following pairs of structures by the aneurysm most likely explains his hoarseness and dysphagia?
options: Left phrenic nerve and trachea
Thoracic duct and left sympathetic trunk
Left recurrent laryngeal nerve and esophagus
Left brachiocephalic vein and left vagus nerve
approach: Link hoarseness to the vocal cords, which are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerves.
Recall that the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch next to the ligamentum arteriosum.
Link trouble swallowing to the esophagus, which lies just to the right of the arch.
questions.why: The left vagus nerve gives off the left recurrent laryngeal nerve as it crosses the aortic arch. The nerve hooks under the arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum and climbs back up in the groove between the trachea and esophagus to supply most of the muscles of the larynx. An arch aneurysm can stretch or compress it, causing left vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness. The esophagus lies right next to the arch and the descending aorta, so a large aneurysm can also compress it and cause dysphagia.
whyNot: The phrenic nerve controls the diaphragm, so compressing it paralyzes a hemidiaphragm. It does not cause hoarseness, and tracheal compression causes cough and stridor, not trouble swallowing.
Compression of the sympathetic trunk can cause Horner syndrome, and duct injury can cause chylothorax. Neither causes hoarseness or trouble swallowing.
Correct.
A compressed brachiocephalic vein causes swelling of the left arm and face. It does not explain trouble swallowing solid food.

questions.stem: His increased serum creatinine concentration and mild proteinuria are attributed to long-standing hypertension without a malignant phase. Which of the following changes is most likely present in the walls of his small renal arterioles?
options: Hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis
Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis
Necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis
approach: Note the setting: years of moderate (benign) hypertension, not a hypertensive emergency.
Recall that chronic pressure pushes plasma proteins into arteriolar walls and stimulates extra matrix.
The result is pink, glassy wall thickening that narrows the lumen: hyaline arteriolosclerosis, which causes nephrosclerosis.
questions.why: In long-standing benign hypertension, and also in diabetes, plasma proteins leak through injured endothelium into the walls of small arterioles, and smooth muscle cells lay down extra basement membrane. The wall becomes thick, pink, and glassy on H&E stain, and the lumen narrows. In the kidney, the resulting ischemia shrinks glomeruli and tubules. This is benign nephrosclerosis, which causes a slow rise in creatinine and mild proteinuria.
whyNot: Concentric layers of smooth muscle and basement membrane, often with fibrinoid necrosis, are seen in malignant hypertension, usually with pressures above 180/120 mm Hg and acute organ damage.
Correct.
Monckeberg sclerosis is calcification in the media of medium-sized muscular arteries in older people. It does not narrow the lumen or damage the kidney.
Granulomatous inflammation that destroys vessel walls is seen in vasculitis, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis. It is not caused by hypertension.

questions.stem: Three weeks later, he develops sudden tearing chest pain and collapses. Blood pressure is 76/50 mm Hg. Physical examination shows jugular venous distention and muffled heart sounds. The ascending aorta has dissected and ruptured. Into which of the following spaces is blood most likely accumulating?
options: Pericardial cavity
Left pleural cavity
Posterior mediastinum
Superior mediastinum
approach: Recognize Beck triad: low blood pressure, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds point to cardiac tamponade.
Recall that the ascending aorta begins inside the pericardial sac.
Blood from an ascending aortic rupture fills the pericardial cavity, between the parietal and visceral layers of serous pericardium.
questions.why: The pericardial cavity is the thin space between the parietal and visceral layers of serous pericardium. Because the fibrous pericardium does not stretch quickly, sudden bleeding into this space raises its pressure and squeezes the heart, especially the thin-walled right side, so the ventricles cannot fill in diastole. Stroke volume and blood pressure fall, venous pressure rises, and the fluid muffles the heart sounds. The same picture follows a stab wound to the heart or rupture of the free wall after a myocardial infarction.
whyNot: Correct.
Rupture of the descending thoracic aorta often bleeds into the left pleural cavity. That causes hypotension and a hemothorax, but not distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds.
Bleeding there collects around the descending aorta and esophagus, outside the pericardial sac, so it does not cause tamponade. His rupture is in the ascending aorta, which lies inside the sac.
The aortic arch and great vessels lie in the superior mediastinum, outside the pericardial sac. Bleeding there does not produce Beck triad.

case: A 4-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of episodes of perioral cyanosis during crying and feeding. She was born at term after a normal pregnancy. Physical examination shows a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border. Oxygen saturation is 82% on room air (normal 95 to 100%). Chest x-ray shows a boot-shaped heart with reduced lung markings. Echocardiography shows a large ventricular septal defect, an aorta that sits over the defect, narrowing of the right ventricular outflow tract below the pulmonary valve, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Diagnosis: tetralogy of Fallot.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms best explains her cyanosis?
options: Right-to-left shunt across the VSD because flow to the lungs is obstructed
Left-to-right shunt across the VSD because left ventricular pressure is higher
Left-to-right shunt across a patent ductus because aortic pressure is higher
Two parallel circuits with no mixing because the great arteries are switched
approach: Note the low saturation with reduced lung markings: less blood is reaching the lungs.
Identify the obstruction: right ventricular outflow narrowing raises right ventricular pressure.
With a large VSD, deoxygenated blood takes the easier path into the overriding aorta, a right-to-left shunt.
questions.why: In tetralogy of Fallot, narrowing of the right ventricular outflow tract makes it hard for blood to reach the lungs. Right ventricular pressure rises to match or exceed left ventricular pressure, so deoxygenated blood crosses the large VSD into the overriding aorta. This right-to-left shunt sends unoxygenated blood to the body and causes cyanosis. The more severe the outflow obstruction, the larger the shunt and the worse the cyanosis.
whyNot: Correct.
A left-to-right shunt sends oxygenated blood back to the lungs. It increases lung markings and does not cause cyanosis early on, as in an isolated VSD.
Flow from the aorta into the pulmonary artery through a patent ductus returns oxygenated blood to the lungs. It does not cause cyanosis unless pulmonary hypertension later reverses it.
Parallel circuits are the problem in transposition of the great arteries, where the aorta arises from the right ventricle. Her echo shows an overriding aorta, not transposition.

questions.stem: During an episode of severe cyanosis, her mother draws the infant's knees up to her chest, and the cyanosis improves. Older children with this defect squat for the same reason. Which of the following best explains this improvement?
options: It lowers systemic vascular resistance, so more blood enters the aorta
It lowers venous return, so the right ventricle ejects less blood
It raises systemic resistance, so less blood crosses the VSD
It relaxes the outflow tract muscle, so pulmonary resistance falls
approach: See the VSD as a fork: right ventricular blood goes to the lungs or into the aorta, whichever path resists less.
Flexing the legs kinks the femoral arteries and raises systemic vascular resistance.
Higher aortic resistance pushes more right ventricular blood through the narrowed outflow tract to the lungs, so oxygenation improves.
questions.why: The direction of flow across her VSD depends on the balance between resistance to pulmonary flow and resistance to systemic flow. Pulling the knees to the chest, or squatting, compresses the femoral arteries and raises systemic vascular resistance. With a higher pressure in the aorta, less deoxygenated blood crosses from the right ventricle into the aorta and more goes to the lungs. Anything that lowers systemic resistance, such as exercise or a hot bath, does the opposite.
whyNot: Lower systemic resistance makes the aorta an easier path for right ventricular blood, which increases the right-to-left shunt and worsens cyanosis.
Squatting tends to increase venous return from the legs. Less right ventricular filling would also not send more blood to the lungs.
Correct.
Spasm of the outflow tract can trigger a spell, but leg position does not relax it. The benefit comes from the systemic side of the circulation.

topics: Systemic vascular resistance and shunt direction

questions.stem: Before surgery, a catheter is advanced from the inferior vena cava into the right atrium and then directly into the hypertrophied ventricle with the narrowed outflow tract. Which of the following valves does the catheter cross?
options: Mitral valve
Tricuspid valve
Pulmonary valve
Aortic valve
approach: Identify the chamber: the hypertrophied chamber with a narrowed outflow tract in tetralogy of Fallot is the right ventricle.
The catheter is moving from the right atrium to the right ventricle.
Name the right atrioventricular valve: the tricuspid valve.
questions.why: The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve, with three leaflets held by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles of the right ventricle. A venous catheter passes from the inferior vena cava into the right atrium and through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. In tetralogy of Fallot, right ventricular pressure equals left ventricular and aortic pressure because the large VSD joins the two ventricles and the outflow tract is narrow.
whyNot: The mitral valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle. A catheter from the inferior vena cava would reach it only by crossing the atrial septum.
Correct.
The pulmonary valve guards the exit from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk. The catheter would cross it only after leaving the right ventricle.
The aortic valve guards the exit from the left ventricle. It is reached from the arterial side or by crossing the septum.

questions.stem: Before birth, oxygenated blood from the placenta entered her right atrium through the inferior vena cava and passed directly to the left atrium. Which of the following correctly names this structure and the reason it normally closes after birth?
options: Ductus arteriosus; rising oxygen and falling prostaglandin E2 constrict it
Ductus venosus; flow in the umbilical vein stops when the cord is clamped
Foramen ovale; falling oxygen levels constrict the septum primum
Foramen ovale; left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure
approach: Trace fetal blood: inferior vena cava to right atrium, then across the atrial septum to the left atrium.
Name the opening in the atrial septum: the foramen ovale.
At birth, lung blood flow rises, more blood returns to the left atrium, and left atrial pressure pushes the septum primum flap shut.
questions.why: In the fetus, the crista dividens (the lower edge of the septum secundum) directs oxygen-rich inferior vena cava blood through the foramen ovale into the left atrium, so it bypasses the airless lungs. At birth the lungs expand, pulmonary resistance falls, pulmonary venous return to the left atrium rises, and placental flow into the right side stops. Left atrial pressure then exceeds right atrial pressure and presses the septum primum against the septum secundum. The opening later seals to form the fossa ovalis.
whyNot: This is how the ductus arteriosus closes, but the ductus joins the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. It does not carry blood between the atria.
The ductus venosus carries umbilical vein blood past the liver into the inferior vena cava. It does not connect the two atria.
The foramen ovale is the correct structure, but it closes by pressure, with no muscle to constrict. Oxygen level is the trigger for closing the ductus arteriosus.
Correct.

topics: Changes in the circulation at birth

dx: Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy (dilated) with left and then right heart failure
case: A 47-year-old woman who grew up in a mud-walled house in rural Bolivia comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of worsening dyspnea with paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and a 1-month history of leg swelling. Physical examination shows bibasilar crackles, an S3 gallop, jugular venous distention, tender hepatomegaly, and pitting edema of the legs. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25% (normal 55 to 70%) and an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 58 mm Hg (normal 15 to 30 mm Hg). Coronary angiography is normal. Serum albumin is 4.0 g/dL (3.5 to 5.0 g/dL). Two serologic tests for Trypanosoma cruzi are positive. Diagnosis: chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy with heart failure.

questions.stem: By which of the following routes was Trypanosoma cruzi most likely transmitted to her during childhood?
options: Tsetse fly saliva injected during a bite
Sand fly saliva injected during a bite
Triatomine bug feces rubbed into a bite
Anopheles mosquito saliva injected during a bite
approach: Link the setting, a rural home with mud walls in Latin America, to the insects that live in wall cracks.
Name the vector of Trypanosoma cruzi: triatomine (reduviid, kissing) bugs.
Recall the route: the bug defecates while feeding, and the person rubs infected feces into the bite or the conjunctiva.
questions.why: Trypanosoma cruzi is carried by triatomine (reduviid or kissing) bugs that hide in cracks in mud walls and thatched roofs and feed at night. The parasite is in the bug's feces, not its saliva, and enters through the bite wound or mucous membranes when the person scratches or rubs the area. Years later, about 20 to 30% of infected people develop chronic disease, most often a dilated cardiomyopathy, with megaesophagus or megacolon in some.
whyNot: Tsetse flies in Africa carry Trypanosoma brucei, which causes African sleeping sickness. They do not live in the Americas.
Sand flies transmit Leishmania species, which cause cutaneous and visceral leishmaniasis.
Correct.
Female Anopheles mosquitoes transmit Plasmodium species, which cause malaria.

questions.stem: Her dyspnea preceded the leg edema, jugular venous distention, and hepatomegaly by several months. Which of the following mechanisms best explains how her left ventricular failure led to these right-sided findings?
options: Pulmonary venous congestion raised right ventricular afterload
Occlusion of the right coronary artery caused a right ventricular infarct
Low plasma oncotic pressure from protein loss let fluid leave the capillaries
A stiff, thickened pericardium limited filling of the right ventricle
approach: Start on the left: a failing left ventricle raises left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure, which causes her breathlessness and crackles.
Follow the pressure backward: pulmonary artery pressure rises (58 mm Hg), raising right ventricular afterload.
The right ventricle fails, so systemic venous pressure rises, causing raised jugular venous pressure, liver congestion, and leg edema.
questions.why: Left ventricular failure is the most common cause of right ventricular failure. When the left ventricle cannot empty, left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures rise, and the pulmonary arteries must work at higher pressure to push blood through the lungs. The thin-walled right ventricle tolerates this afterload poorly and eventually fails. Systemic venous pressure then rises, causing raised jugular venous pressure, a congested liver, and dependent edema.
whyNot: Correct.
Her coronary angiogram is normal, so there was no right coronary occlusion.
Her albumin is normal. Low oncotic pressure, as in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis, causes edema without raised jugular venous pressure.
Constrictive pericarditis limits filling of both ventricles and would not explain a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25%.

topics: Pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease

questions.stem: In a healthy heart, an increase in end-diastolic volume increases stroke volume, but her dilated ventricle gains little stroke volume from the same increase in filling. Which of the following is the main cellular basis of this length-tension relationship in a normal ventricle?
options: Stretch shortens the sarcomeres, so more myosin heads bind to the thin filaments
Stretch releases norepinephrine from cardiac nerve endings, which raises contractility
Stretch lowers wall tension, so afterload falls and the ventricle empties more fully
Stretch sets better filament overlap and makes troponin C more sensitive to calcium
approach: Name the principle: the Frank-Starling mechanism, where preload sets stroke volume.
Go to the sarcomere: stretch moves resting sarcomere length toward the optimum and increases the calcium sensitivity of the myofilaments.
Apply it to her: a failing ventricle has a flattened curve, so extra filling mostly raises filling pressure and congestion.
questions.why: When the ventricle fills more, each myocyte is stretched. In the normal working range this brings the sarcomere closer to its optimal length, and it increases the calcium sensitivity of troponin C, so the same calcium transient produces more force. The ventricle therefore ejects more, matching output to venous return beat by beat. In a dilated, failing ventricle the curve is flat, so extra preload adds congestion with little gain in stroke volume.
whyNot: Filling stretches the sarcomeres, it does not shorten them. In the normal working range, stretch brings sarcomere length closer to the optimum for force.
Norepinephrine raises contractility through beta-1 receptors, but stretch does not release it. The Frank-Starling effect works in a denervated, transplanted heart.
By the Laplace relationship, a larger chamber has higher wall tension for the same pressure, so afterload on each fiber rises with dilation.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her low cardiac output decreases perfusion pressure in the renal afferent arterioles, and juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Which of the following sequences correctly describes the subsequent steps leading to aldosterone release?
options: ACE converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, then renin converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II
Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, then ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II
Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin II, then ACE converts angiotensin II to aldosterone
Renin converts angiotensin I to angiotensinogen, then ACE converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin II
approach: Identify the trigger: low afferent arteriolar pressure and less sodium chloride at the macula densa cause renin release.
Place each enzyme: renin cleaves liver-made angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, and ACE, mainly on lung endothelium, converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
Angiotensin II acts on the zona glomerulosa to release aldosterone.
questions.why: Juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole release renin when renal perfusion pressure falls, when the macula densa senses less sodium chloride, or with sympathetic stimulation through beta-1 receptors. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen, made by the liver, to angiotensin I. Angiotensin-converting enzyme, abundant on pulmonary capillary endothelium, converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts arterioles and stimulates the zona glomerulosa to release aldosterone, which increases sodium and water retention and worsens edema in heart failure.
whyNot: The enzymes are reversed. Renin acts first, on angiotensinogen, and ACE acts second.
Correct.
Renin makes angiotensin I, not angiotensin II. Aldosterone is a steroid made from cholesterol in the adrenal cortex, not a product of ACE.
Angiotensinogen is the starting substrate made by the liver. It is not a product of renin.

dx: Lyme carditis with complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block
case: A 26-year-old man from Connecticut comes to the emergency department in August because of a 2-day history of lightheadedness and one episode of syncope. Five weeks ago, after hiking, he had an expanding erythematous rash with central clearing on his thigh that resolved without treatment. Pulse is 42/min and blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg. The ECG shows regular P waves at 84/min and regular, narrow QRS complexes (0.08 s; normal below 0.12 s) at 42/min, with no fixed relationship between them. Serologic testing confirms Lyme disease. Diagnosis: Lyme carditis with complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of his condition?
options: Rickettsia rickettsii
Borrelia burgdorferi
Treponema pallidum
Ehrlichia chaffeensis
approach: Recognize erythema migrans: an expanding red rash with central clearing after a tick exposure.
Link it to Lyme disease, which in the northeastern United States is carried by Ixodes ticks.
Recall that early disseminated Lyme disease can cause carditis, most often as AV block.
questions.why: Lyme disease is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, carried by Ixodes ticks in the northeastern and upper midwestern United States. Erythema migrans marks early local infection. Weeks later the organism can spread to the heart, nerves, and joints. Lyme carditis most often causes AV block that can change quickly in degree, and it usually resolves with antibiotics, sometimes after temporary pacing.
whyNot: R. rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever: fever, headache, and a rash that starts on the wrists and ankles and spreads to the trunk, including the palms and soles.
Correct.
T. pallidum causes syphilis. Its main cardiovascular effect is tertiary syphilitic aortitis, which damages the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta years after infection.
Ehrlichia is spread by the lone star tick and causes fever, low white cell and platelet counts, and raised liver enzymes. It does not cause erythema migrans or heart block.

questions.stem: His P waves continue at a regular rate of 84/min although none are conducted to the ventricles. Which of the following correctly names the structure that sets this atrial rate and its location?
options: AV node, in the interatrial septum near the coronary sinus opening
Bundle of His, in the membranous part of the interventricular septum
Purkinje fibers, under the endocardium of the right ventricle
SA node, in the right atrial wall near the superior vena cava
approach: Note that each P wave is an atrial depolarization, so something above the block is firing at 84/min.
Recall the fastest intrinsic pacemaker: the SA node, at about 60 to 100/min.
Locate it: in the wall of the right atrium where the superior vena cava enters, at the top of the crista terminalis.
questions.why: The SA node lies in the wall of the right atrium where the superior vena cava enters, at the upper end of the crista terminalis. Its cells depolarize on their own faster than any other cardiac tissue, at about 60 to 100/min, so they set the rate of the whole heart in health. In complete heart block, the SA node keeps driving the atria normally, but its impulses cannot reach the ventricles.
whyNot: The AV node is the structure most often blocked in Lyme carditis. It does not set the atrial rate, and its own rate is only about 40 to 60/min.
The bundle of His carries impulses from the AV node to the bundle branches. It does not drive atrial depolarization.
Purkinje fibers spread the impulse through the ventricles. Their intrinsic rate is about 20 to 40/min, and they do not drive the atria.
Correct.

questions.stem: His QRS complexes are narrow (0.08 s) and occur at 42/min, independent of the P waves. Which of the following best describes the origin and spread of this escape rhythm?
options: Ventricular depolarization spreads from a focus above the bundle branch split
Ventricular repolarization spreads from a focus above the bundle branch split
Ventricular depolarization spreads cell to cell from a Purkinje fiber focus
Atrial depolarization spreads backward from a focus in the AV node
approach: Recall that the QRS complex records ventricular depolarization.
A narrow QRS means the impulse entered the ventricles through the His bundle and spread rapidly through both bundle branches and the Purkinje system.
A rate of about 40 to 60/min with a narrow QRS fits a junctional escape pacemaker in the AV junction or His bundle.
questions.why: The QRS complex records depolarization of the ventricles. When the impulse starts at or above the His bundle, it spreads through the fast His-Purkinje system and the QRS stays narrow, below 0.12 s. An escape focus in the ventricular muscle or distal Purkinje fibers has to spread slowly from cell to cell and gives a wide QRS. His narrow QRS at 42/min points to a junctional escape rhythm below a block in the AV node, the usual site of block in Lyme carditis.
whyNot: Correct.
Ventricular repolarization is shown by the T wave. The QRS complex records ventricular depolarization.
An escape beat from the Purkinje fibers or ventricular muscle spreads slowly through muscle, giving a wide QRS of 0.12 s or more and a rate of about 20 to 40/min.
Atrial depolarization is shown by the P wave. His P waves come from the SA node and are unrelated to the QRS complexes.

questions.stem: Intravenous atropine is administered, and his P-wave rate increases from 84/min to 112/min. Atropine blocked which of the following effects of vagal acetylcholine on SA node cells?
options: Activation of beta-1 receptors that raise cAMP and speed up phase 4
Activation of nicotinic receptors that open sodium channels in nodal cells
Activation of M2 receptors that open potassium channels and slow phase 4
Activation of M3 receptors that raise IP3 and release stored calcium
approach: Recall that atropine blocks muscarinic receptors, so the rate rise means vagal tone was slowing the SA node.
Name the cardiac muscarinic receptor: M2, coupled to Gi.
M2 activation opens acetylcholine-sensitive potassium channels and lowers cAMP, which reduces the funny current and slows phase 4 depolarization.
questions.why: Vagal fibers release acetylcholine onto M2 muscarinic receptors in the SA and AV nodes. Through Gi, the beta-gamma subunits open acetylcholine-sensitive potassium channels, which make the resting potential more negative, and the alpha subunit lowers cAMP, which reduces the funny current. Both effects slow phase 4 depolarization, so the node takes longer to reach threshold and the rate falls. Atropine blocks M2 receptors and removes this brake.
whyNot: Beta-1 activation by norepinephrine is the sympathetic effect, and it speeds the heart. Atropine does not block beta-1 receptors.
Nicotinic receptors are found at autonomic ganglia and the neuromuscular junction. Postganglionic vagal fibers act on muscarinic receptors at the SA node.
Correct.
M3 receptors act through Gq and IP3 in smooth muscle and glands. The heart uses M2 receptors, which act through Gi.

dx: Wet beriberi (thiamine deficiency) with high-output heart failure, and deep vein thrombosis, in a woman with pancreatic cancer
case: A 68-year-old woman with metastatic adenocarcinoma of the pancreas has had poor oral intake and frequent vomiting for 3 months. She now has dyspnea, leg edema, and numbness and burning pain in both feet. Her pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 112/48 mm Hg. Physical examination shows warm skin and bounding peripheral pulses. Echocardiography shows an end-diastolic volume of 160 mL and an end-systolic volume of 60 mL. Serum lactate is 4.1 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2 mmol/L). She is admitted to the hospital and confined to bed. On hospital day 4, her left calf becomes swollen. Ultrasound shows a deep vein thrombosis in the left femoral and popliteal veins. She is later found to be heterozygous for factor V Leiden. Diagnosis: wet beriberi with high-output heart failure, and a deep vein thrombosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is closest to her cardiac output?
options: 1.1 L/min
6.6 L/min
11.0 L/min
17.6 L/min
approach: Find stroke volume: end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume, 160 mL minus 60 mL, which is 100 mL.
Multiply by heart rate: 100 mL times 110/min is 11,000 mL/min.
Convert and judge: 11.0 L/min is about twice the normal resting output of about 5 L/min, which fits high-output failure.
questions.why: Cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate. Stroke volume is the end-diastolic volume minus the end-systolic volume, here 100 mL, so her output is 100 mL times 110/min, or 11.0 L/min. Her ejection fraction is 100 divided by 160, about 63%, so the pump itself is not weak. In wet beriberi, peripheral vasodilation lowers systemic vascular resistance and the heart must pump a very high output, which over time leads to failure with congestion.
whyNot: This misplaces the decimal when converting units. Stroke volume is 100 mL, and 100 mL times 110/min is 11,000 mL/min, which is 11.0 L/min.
This multiplies the end-systolic volume (60 mL) by the heart rate. End-systolic volume is the blood left in the ventricle after the beat, not the amount ejected.
Correct.
This multiplies the end-diastolic volume (160 mL) by the heart rate. Not all of the end-diastolic volume is ejected.

questions.stem: Her increased serum lactate and her cardiac and neurologic findings result from deficiency of a cofactor required by several enzymes of energy metabolism. Which of the following reactions is most directly impaired?
options: Methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA
Pyruvate to acetyl-CoA
Alanine to pyruvate by transamination
Pyruvate to oxaloacetate
approach: Name the missing cofactor in wet beriberi: thiamine pyrophosphate, made from vitamin B1.
List the enzymes that need it: pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase, and transketolase.
Link pyruvate dehydrogenase failure to her findings: pyruvate is shunted to lactate, and aerobic ATP production falls in heart and nerve.
questions.why: Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, which converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA so it can enter the citric acid cycle. It is also needed by alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase. Without it, pyruvate builds up and is turned into lactate, and tissues that rely on glucose oxidation, such as nerves and heart, cannot make enough ATP. Poor intake, vomiting, and alcohol use are common causes of deficiency, and giving glucose before thiamine can make it worse.
whyNot: This reaction needs vitamin B12 (adenosylcobalamin). B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and spinal cord disease, not high-output heart failure.
Correct.
Transamination needs pyridoxal phosphate from vitamin B6. B6 deficiency causes neuropathy, cheilosis, and sideroblastic anemia.
Pyruvate carboxylase needs biotin. Biotin deficiency is rare and causes dermatitis and hair loss.

questions.stem: Which of the following components of Virchow triad best explain the formation of her deep vein thrombosis?
options: Endothelial injury and turbulent flow
Endothelial injury and venous stasis
Venous stasis and hypercoagulability
Turbulent flow and hypercoagulability
approach: List the triad: endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), and hypercoagulability.
Match her risks: bed rest causes venous stasis; pancreatic cancer and factor V Leiden cause hypercoagulability.
Pick the pair that matches the case.
questions.why: Virchow triad names three factors that lead to thrombosis: endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow, and hypercoagulability. In the deep leg veins, slow flow from immobility is the main flow problem, because the calf muscle pump stops working. Mucin-secreting adenocarcinomas such as pancreatic cancer release procoagulant factors, including tissue factor, and factor V Leiden adds an inherited hypercoagulable state. Her deep vein thrombosis therefore reflects stasis and hypercoagulability.
whyNot: These two drive thrombosis in arteries and the heart, such as on a ruptured plaque or an aneurysm. In the deep leg veins of an immobile patient, slow flow is the main problem.
Stasis applies to her, but nothing in the case points to injury of the vein wall, such as trauma, surgery, or a catheter. This pair also leaves out her cancer and factor V Leiden.
Correct.
Her cancer and factor V Leiden make her blood hypercoagulable, but blood in the deep leg veins of a bedbound patient moves slowly, which is stasis, not turbulence.

questions.stem: Factor V Leiden is a single amino acid substitution in factor V. Which of the following best explains how this variant increases her risk of thrombosis?
options: Factor Va resists activated protein C
Factor Va binds tissue factor more tightly
Factor V is no longer able to bind antithrombin
Factor V is made in greater amounts by the liver
approach: Recall the normal brake: activated protein C, with protein S, cleaves and inactivates factors Va and VIIIa.
Identify the variant: factor V Leiden changes arginine 506, the site where activated protein C cuts factor Va.
Factor Va stays active longer, so more thrombin is made and clots form more easily.
questions.why: Factor V Leiden is a point mutation in the factor V gene that replaces arginine with glutamine at position 506, one of the sites where activated protein C cleaves factor Va. Factor Va therefore resists inactivation, keeps supporting the prothrombinase complex, and more thrombin is made. It is the most common inherited thrombophilia in people of European descent and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Heterozygotes have a several-fold higher risk of venous thrombosis, which adds to risks such as cancer and immobility.
whyNot: Correct.
Tissue factor binds factor VII to start the extrinsic pathway. Factor V does not bind tissue factor.
Antithrombin mainly inhibits thrombin and factor Xa, and heparin speeds this up. Antithrombin deficiency is a separate inherited thrombophilia.
The Leiden variant does not raise the amount of factor V. Increased levels of a clotting factor describe other risks, such as high factor VIII.
